EARLY DETECTION
● Thymic hyperplasia or 
thymoma
● History of autoimmune 
disorders
● Genetic susceptibility: 
usually not inherited
● Reduce infection exposure
● Avoid overheating and 
excessive stress
● Ask the provider before 
taking any new prescription 
or OTC drug
● Take medications exactly 
as prescribed
● Balance activity with 
planned rest
● Plan tasks and meals 
during stronger periods
● Maintain nutrition and 
follow-up care
● Weakness worsens with 
activity and improves with 
rest
● Ptosis or diplopia often 
appears first
● Reports of speech, 
chewing, or swallowing 
problems
● Weak cough or dyspnea 
requires emergency care

03 CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
OCULAR
● Ptosis
● Diplopia
BULBAR / FACIAL
● Dysarthria
● Dysphagia
● Facial weakness
LIMB / AXIAL
● Proximal muscle weakness
● Neck weakness
RESPIRATORY
● Dyspnea
● Weak cough
● Myasthenic crisis
Hallmark: Muscle weakness worsens with 
activity and improves with rest.
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

05 MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
01
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine, pyridostigmine)
Relieve symptoms only and do not change the disease course. Too much can cause cholinergic 
crisis.
02
Immunosuppressants: prednisone, azathioprine, rituximab
High-dose steroids can briefly worsen weakness, so they are often started low. Azathioprine takes 
months to work; rituximab is mainly for MuSK+ or hard-to-treat MG.
03
Surgical removal of the thymus gland (thymectomy)
For thymoma and for many adults with AChR+ generalized MG. Can improve symptoms and reduce 
the need for steroids.
04
Therapeutic plasma exchange and IVIG
Plasma exchange removes harmful antibodies from the blood. Both work quickly but last only weeks, 
so they are used for crises, severe flares, or before surgery.
05 Myasthenic crisis managementICU care, intubation and mechanical ventilation if breathing fails, plus plasma exchange or IVIG.
Source: Narayanaswami et al., 2021

06 MEDICATION MANAGEMENT / NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
MEDICATION MANAGEMENT
Consistency
Give doses on time to sustain muscle strength and 
prevent sudden weakness. 
Timing
Administer pyridostigmine 30–60 minutes before 
meals to optimize chewing/swallowing and reduce 
aspiration risk.
Contraindications
Avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta-
blockers, and magnesium, which can precipitate a 
crisis.
Check Breathing
Monitor vital capacity and NIF to catch respiratory 
failure early (Claytor et al., 2023).
Choking Prevention
Sit the patient upright in high Fowler's position 
during meals and provide soft foods to protect the 
airway and prevent aspiration.
Crisis Readiness
Keep suction, oxygen, and emergency airway 
equipment at the bedside, and have atropine ready 
if a cholinergic crisis occurs.
Safety
Weak grip raises burn and fall risk (e.g., dropping 
hot tea). Use lidded cups and assist with walking.
NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES

07 PATIENT AND FAMILY EDUCATION
PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION
what they need to know before they go home
01
Know myasthenic vs. 
cholinergic crisis signs
Both look similar but require opposite treatment, so 
mistaking one for the other can be dangerous (Barber, 
2017).
MYASTHENIC CRISIS
Too little medication
CHOLINERGIC CRISIS
Too much medication
Same weakness  →  opposite treatment
02
Time medications around 
meals & activities
Anticholinesterase drugs wear off quickly, 
so dosing before meals or key tasks gives 
patients the most usable strength when 
they need it.
03
Build self-management 
skills, not just knowledge
Use the teach-back method to ensure 
understanding. Don’t just give handouts; 
make sure you’re actually educating.
04
Screen for depression & 
anxiety
About a third of MG patients report 
depression or anxiety (Marbin et al., 2022; 
Nadali et al., 2023).
05
Include family as much as 
possible
Family members often become primary 
caregivers and need to know which 
symptoms to watch for and how to manage 
medications.

08 DISCHARGE PLANNING / HOME CARE
DISCHARGE PLANNING & HOME CARE
discharge starts on day one
ADMISSION
01
Start discharge 
planning on 
admission
Early assessment lets the 
team catch gaps before 
they escalate and 
complicate discharge.
DURING THE STAY
02
Teach and 
practice self-
care skills
Hands-on practice with 
medication administration 
and symptom monitoring, 
reinforced throughout the 
stay.
BEFORE DISCHARGE
03
Confirm the 
patient can self-
manage
Verify actual ability to 
perform tasks, not just 
understanding.
DISCHARGE DAY
04
Give structured 
instructions
A consistent format for 
medications, warning signs, 
and follow-up reduces the 
chance something gets 
missed in the rush to leave.
AFTER DISCHARGE
05
Schedule and 
track follow-up
Regular check-ins give the 
team a chance to catch 
worsening weakness early.
ALL ALONG THE WAY
06
Prepare caregivers, not just the patient
Caregiver burden is common in MG, so families must be prepared as much as patients are (Marbin et al., 2022).
HOME SAFETY Remove rugs and clutter, add grab bars and a shower chair, use lidded mugs for hot drinks, plan rest before tasks, and keep a phone within reach.

09 NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 1
01
A
B
C
D
A client with myasthenia gravis takes pyridostigmine. The client 
tells the nurse, "By the end of dinner I can barely chew or 
swallow." What is the nurse's best response?
"Try eating your largest meal right before bed when you are most relaxed."
"Take your pyridostigmine about 30 to 60 minutes before meals."
"Switch to a full liquid diet to avoid choking."
"Skip your dose before dinner so the medication does not upset your 
stomach."

10 NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION 2
02
A client with myasthenia gravis took extra doses of 
pyridostigmine at home because of increasing weakness. The 
client now has worsening muscle weakness, excessive 
salivation, sweating, abdominal cramping, and a heart rate of 52. 
Which action should the nurse anticipate?
A
B
C
D
Administer an additional dose of pyridostigmine
Prepare the client for an emergency thymectomy
Hold the anticholinesterase medication and have atropine available
Encourage the client to increase activity to rebuild muscle strength
